items.attribution: Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech, December 1886
items.exemplar: (a) New South supporters promised that railroads, mills, and Northern capital would industrialize the South — iron and steel in Birmingham, textile mills across the Carolina Piedmont, tobacco factories in North Carolina — closing the wealth gap with the North. (b) Most Southerners remained poor farmers trapped by sharecropping and the crop-lien system: landless tenants bought supplies on credit at inflated prices and paid in cotton, ending each year deeper in debt — what critics called wage slavery in a new form. (c) The break was only partial. Real industry did grow, but the labor system echoed slavery's coercion, the capital came mostly from the North, and the South stayed the nation's poorest region — abolition had ended slavery without ending its economic logic.

parts.prompt: Identify one economic change that supporters of the 'New South' creed promised for the region.
Explain how the sharecropping and crop-lien system contradicted the creed's promises.
Evaluate the extent to which the New South represented a break from the Old South.

items.stimulus_text: 'There was a South of slavery and secession — that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom — that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.' (Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech to New York businessmen, December 1886)

items.attribution: Department-store newspaper advertisement, 1890 (Wikimedia Commons, public domain)
items.exemplar: (a) Department stores such as Macy's, Marshall Field's, and Wanamaker's introduced fixed prices, advertising, and brand names, and made shopping itself a leisure activity. (b) Electric streetcars let families live farther from their workplaces, creating streetcar suburbs that separated home from work and made homeownership — the class's defining aspiration — achievable for more families. (c) The claim is well supported. The same clerks and professionals who bought the new economy's goods used their schooling, leisure, and reform organizations — women's clubs, temperance unions — to demand pure food, clean cities, and honest government in the 1900s: they bought the system's promises, then tried to fix its abuses.

parts.prompt: Identify one way department stores changed American shopping in the Gilded Age.
Explain how electric streetcars changed where middle-class families lived.
Evaluate the claim that the Gilded Age middle class became 'Progressivism's foot soldiers.'
